Switzler Hall was originally called Scientific Hall and later used as the Agricultural Building. Renamed in 1909 for Colonel William Franklin Switzler, a prominent Missouri Statesman editor, Boone County historian, and university curator supporter. It houses a three-story silo in its interior.
Geological Sciences Building was built in 1965 to house the expanding department.
8th Street Circle is a prominent landscaped focal point and display garden located on the University of Missouri campus in Columbia, Missouri.
Peace Park is a historic green space on the northern edge of the University of Missouri campus that was unofficially named in 1970 to honor victims of anti-war protests.
Gannett Hall was designed in 1976. Named after Gannett Company, a major media organization that helped finance the construction of the building.
Reynolds Journalism Institute was launched in 2004 using a landmark $31 million grant from the Donald W. Reynolds Foundation.

Neff Hall is the world's first dedicated building for a school of journalism and its daily newspaper.

Pickard Hall is a historic 1892 red-brick building on the Francis Quadrangle that was closed in 2013 and slated for demolition due to lingering radioactive contamination from early 20th-century radium experiments.
Jefferson Statue was installed in 2001.

The Columns. The David R. Francis Quadrangle Historic District—known as The Quad. Built between 1840-1843, it was the university's first and main building. A massive fire destroyed Academic Hall on January 9, 1892.
Swallow Hall was built in 1893 on the Francis Quadrangle and is named after George Clinton Swallow, the university's first professor of geology, chemistry, and agriculture.
Francis Memorial, in front of Jesse Hall from the Columns view. It's a deeply historically significant landmark honoring the 27th Governor of Missouri, David R. Francis.
Stairs between Jesse Hall and Tate Hall.

Tate Hall was built in 1924-1927 to serve as the permanent home for the MU School of Law. It was named in honor of the donors' son Lee Harry Tate, a 1913 graduate of the MU Law School who died young following his service in the U.S. Navy during WWI.
Speaker's Circle is a famous open-air gathering place and designated free-speech zone.

Sinquefield Music Center(Fine Aarts Annex) initially served as a Baptist Student Center, then the university acquired to ease space shortages for the music department. In 2018, the Fine Arts Annes was torn down to build the modern Sinquefield Music Center.

Eckles Hall.  It was constructed in 1901 as the Dairy Building, home to the first collegiate dairy husbandry department in Missouri, with ~100 cows and bulls grazing across the street in the area that is now the vetrinary school. Eckles is now home to the College of Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resouces.  It also houses the Mizzou Meat Market and Buck's Ice Cream Shop.
